As we mention even in our counter-comments, this is disingenuous at best. IFF has previously written to telecom authorities with its findings on crowd-sourced complaints in which the public apprised us of alleged net neutrality violations. remedy: Happy Holi to everyone here. Traditionally, Holi is not only a celebration of color and community, but also a marker of a subtle seasonal shift. Around this time, Ayurveda recognizes the movement from **Shishira (late winter)** toward **Vasanta (spring)**. From an Ayurvedic perspective, this period of the year is significant because the Kapha that has gradually accumulated during the colder months begins to **liquefy as temperatures rise**. This transition is why many people experience seasonal patterns around this time-congestion, heaviness, sluggish digestion, or allergies. Ayurveda does not see this as a problem so much as a **predictable phase in the seasonal cycle**. Traditionally, the response during this period was to gently lighten the diet, increase movement, and stimulate digestion so that accumulated Kapha could be cleared naturally. Even Holi itself reflects some of these qualities. The celebration historically involved **movement, warmth, community gathering, and activity**, all of which counterbalance the heaviness of Kapha and mark the beginning of a lighter seasonal rhythm. This broader idea of adjusting our habits according to seasonal shifts is what Ayurveda calls **Ritucharya -** the discipline of aligning food, routine, and activity with the changing qualities of nature. In many modern conversations about Ayurveda, we focus heavily on **prakriti (constitution)**. But classical texts place equal importance on how **seasonal rhythms influence everyone**, regardless of constitution. Because today marks that transition into spring, it feels like an appropriate moment to reflect on how seasonal awareness changes the way Ayurveda is practiced. I’ll actually be hosting an **online masterclass on March 14 exploring Ritucharya and how seasonal transitions like this affect digestion, routine, and daily practices**. According to Ayurveda, rising temperatures tend to aggravate *Pitta dosha*, so this is usually the time I start leaning into cooling herbs and lighter habits. Sharing a few Ayurvedic herbs I personally look into every year around this time, before full-blown summer arrives. **Ayurvedic Herbs That Work Well as the Heat Starts Building:** * **Amla (Indian Gooseberry):** One of my go-to summer staples. It’s naturally cooling and supports digestion and skin, which I find especially helpful once the weather turns harsh. * **Shatavari:** Very grounding and hydrating. I like how it balances the dryness and heat that starts showing up even before summer officially begins. * **Guduchi (Giloy):** Helps the body cope with seasonal changes. I usually think of it as a “transition herb” when winter fades and heat starts creeping in. * **Coriander Seeds:** Simple but effective. Coriander seed water is something I start having as soon as afternoons feel heavier and digestion feels off. * **Fennel Seeds (Saunf):** Cooling and gentle. Chewing a little after meals or having fennel tea feels especially comforting as temperatures rise. * **Mint (Pudina):** Nothing says “summer incoming” like mint. It’s refreshing and instantly calming when the body feels overheated. * **Licorice (Mulethi):** Useful when acidity or dryness shows up early due to changing weather, though I keep it in moderation. **A Few Things I’ve Learned:** * Starting summer habits early makes peak summer much easier to handle. * Cooling herbs work best when paired with lighter foods and proper hydration. * I keep everything mild: teas, infused water, or small doses, especially during this seasonal shift. Historically, roasted dandelion root has been used as a coffee substitute and digestive tonic. Herbal texts often mention that the root contains bitter compounds that may support digestion and liver function. I’ve been digging roots in early spring, washing them, chopping them into small pieces, roasting them in the oven until dark brown, and then grinding them before brewing. The flavor surprised me. problem: Am I crazy for thinking people want to smell like an 11th-century pharmacy in a modern office?
symptoms: Hi everyone, I’m having a bit of a creative crisis and need some brutal, unfiltered feedback from people who actually understand plants and sensory grounding. I’ve been obsessed with the idea of "Functional Scent"—not perfumes, but scents that act as a neuro-mechanical "off-switch." I’ve spent months prototyping these cold-pressed botanical beads. No glues, no synthetics. Just raw herbs like Sandalwood, Agarwood, Frankincense, and a high dose of Borneol. Here’s my dilemma: In my head, the scent of Borneol is this incredible, icy-cold "cognitive wake-up call." It’s sharp, medicinal, and groundi
remedy: Hi everyone, I’m having a bit of a creative crisis and need some brutal, unfiltered feedback from people who actually understand plants and sensory grounding. I’ve been obsessed with the idea of "Functional Scent"—not perfumes, but scents that act as a neuro-mechanical "off-switch." I’ve spent months prototyping these cold-pressed botanical beads. No glues, no synthetics. Just raw herbs like Sandalwood, Agarwood, Frankincense, and a high dose of Borneol. Here’s my dilemma: In my head, the scent of Borneol is this incredible, icy-cold "cognitive wake-up call." It’s sharp, medicinal, and grounding. But as I get closer to finishing the prototype, I’m terrified that in a Western professional setting, this is just a "dealbreaker." I need your honesty on two things: 1. **The "Medicinal" Scent:** Does the idea of a raw, herbal, "pharmacy-like" scent appeal to you for focus? Or would you be embarrassed to wear something that doesn't smell like a typical "spa" or "floral" perfume? Is "medicinal" a scent profile you’d ever embrace? 2. **The "Bead" Stigma:** I’ve tried to make it look industrial and modern to avoid the "Hippy/Boho" stereotype. But be honest—does a bracelet with beads still feel "unprofessional" or too "niche" for you to wear at work? Ultimately, I’m trying to gauge: In North America, would people actually embrace wearing these pill-like botanical beads on their wrists and using their scent as a way to enhance their sensory awareness?
